name: Documented after-tax income: bank FX conversion + SWIFT wire
who: A US citizen who can prove the RMB came from lawful current-account income on which PRC individual income tax was already paid or withheld.
tax_note: No PRC tax arises from converting money that has already borne PRC tax. Additional PRC tax is due only if the underlying income was never taxed.
docs: Passport
Employment contract or service invoice/payment proof
PRC IIT payment record / tax certificate (完税证明 / 纳税记录)
Bank card and account opening documents
Source-of-funds statement for the receiving US bank
steps: Download your personal IIT payment record from the PRC individual income tax app or request a 完税证明 at the tax service hall for the years the balance was earned.
Assemble the income file: contract or invoices, payslips, bank statements showing the credits, and the tax record. Amounts must tie to the balance.
Book a counter appointment at the account-holding branch (foreign-exchange business is not reliably transacted at a machine for this category).
Ask for an executable all-in quote: the USD selling rate applied, the 0.1% commission with its CNY 100/500 floor and cap, and the CNY 120 cable fee.
Complete the FX purchase; keep the exchange memo (水单) — it is the document that proves the conversion was authorised and is needed for any later re-conversion.
Instruct the wire to your own US account. Keep the SWIFT MT103 / remittance advice.
File FBAR (FinCEN 114) by 15 April and Form 8938 with your return if thresholds are met; claim PRC tax on Form 1116.
pros: No USD 50,000 ceiling: the cap is the size of the documented lawful income.
Zero incremental PRC tax once the underlying tax is paid; PRC tax already paid is creditable in the US on Form 1116.
Clean audit trail for both SAFE and the receiving US bank.
cons: Requires tax and income paperwork that many people have never collected.
Counter review is discretionary; a thin file is refused.
You bear the bank's spread, which is not published in advance.

name: Documented income routed through same-name HSBC Global Transfer
who: As R01, but you already hold, or qualify for, own-name HSBC accounts in both China and the US (Private Banking / Premier TRB ≥ CNY 500,000, or Advance).
tax_note: Same tax analysis as R01: conversion of already-taxed income adds no PRC tax.
docs: Everything in R01
HSBC US account in the same name
Eligible HSBC China tier (Private Banking / Premier / Advance) confirmed on both sides
steps: Confirm both accounts are in exactly the same name and that Global Transfer is enabled for the China-US corridor.
Complete the R01 documentation and FX conversion inside HSBC China.

Use Global Transfer to move the USD to your own overseas HSBC account: Free for Private Banking and Premier, USD 20 per transfer for Advance (S06 item 2.2.6.1; note USD 7 under item 2.2.7 is for International Education Payment, not a general remittance).
Keep the transfer confirmation as the audit trail; the receiving bank still needs a source-of-funds note.
File FBAR / Form 8938 / Form 1116 as in R01.
pros: Lowest published fixed fee among documented wire channels ($0 for Private Banking / Premier; $20 for Advance under the Oct 2026 tariff).
Same-bank transfer may reduce correspondent-bank deductions (third-party charges remain excluded under Important Note 7).
cons: Requires an eligible HSBC relationship on both sides; Premier preferential tariff requires TRB ≥ CNY 500,000 (Important Note 3).
The spread on the CNY→USD leg is unchanged and remains the dominant, unverified cost.
Account opening for a US person at a Chinese bank is subject to enhanced due diligence.

name: Re-conversion of unused RMB bought with foreign currency (original exchange memo)
who: A US citizen whose RMB came from converting USD or another currency inside China, and who still holds the original exchange memo, within 24 months.
tax_note: Return of previously settled principal; no PRC income tax and no tax voucher is required for this category.
docs: Passport
Original exchange memo (原兑换水单), within 24 months
Bank statements showing the original conversion
steps: Locate the original exchange memo for each conversion you now want to reverse.
Check the date: the memo is valid for 24 months from the exchange date.
Present the passport and memo at the counter and request conversion back to the original currency, then remit.
Keep the new memo; it is the receipt for the outbound leg.
pros: No tax certificate needed — the cleanest documentary path when it applies.
No cap other than the amount of the original conversion.
cons: Only works to the extent you converted FX into RMB in the first place.
Strict 24-month window; expired memos push you back to R01.
You pay a round-trip spread, so this is a recovery route, not a way to move earned income.

name: Passport-only small-amount unused-RMB reconversion at a bank counter
who: A non-domestic individual reconverting unused RMB that was previously exchanged from foreign currency (Guidelines Art. 60 / Hui Fa [2007] Art. 13(2) — NOT a general allowance for salary or savings).
tax_note: No tax at the counter, but the exemption is strictly for reconverting unused RMB previously converted from FX; it does not make untaxed earned income eligible.
docs: Passport
steps: Confirm the RMB represents unused funds from an earlier FX-to-RMB conversion.
Attend a branch counter with your passport.
Request reconversion of no more than the equivalent of USD 500 in one day (or present the original exchange memo within 24 months under R03 for larger unused amounts).
Do not repeat small daily conversions to evade documentation or limits on earned RMB: S01 Art. 7 and S04 prohibit splitting transactions to evade control.
pros: No exchange memo required up to USD 500/day when reconverting unused RMB.
Immediate settlement.
cons: Applies only to previously exchanged unused RMB, NOT earned RMB wages or savings.
USD 500 per day: 20 banking days for USD 10,000 and 800 for USD 400,000; cash spreads are wide, and repeated splitting to evade controls violates S01 Art. 7.

name: Airside pre-departure unused-RMB reconversion at a port-side counter
who: A departing non-domestic individual reconverting unused previously exchanged RMB at a port-side counter before departure (境内关外).
tax_note: Same unused-RMB reconversion rule as R04.
docs: Passport
boarding pass
steps: Reconvert no more than the equivalent of USD 1,000 of unused RMB in a single day at a port-side counter before departure.
Declare the cash to US CBP on FinCEN Form 105 if you arrive with more than USD 10,000 in total (S13).
Do not treat repeated trips as a transfer mechanism.
pros: Higher daily reconversion limit than an onshore counter.
cons: Applies only to unused previously exchanged RMB; USD 1,000 per departure trip.
Requires physically moving cash, with CBP reporting and seizure risk for errors.

name: Withdraw USD cash in China and carry it out
who: Any individual, up to the cash-carrying ceiling.
tax_note: Carrying cash is not a taxable event in itself; it also does not discharge any unpaid PRC or US tax.
docs: Passport
Bank withdrawal slip
Carrying certificate for USD 5,000-10,000
FinCEN Form 105 on arrival above USD 10,000
steps: Convert or withdraw USD banknotes at the counter. Under the 31 Oct 2026 HSBC China tariff (S06 item 2.2.2.1), foreign banknote withdrawal over the counter is Free across Personal segments, with >=3 working days notice required for USD/HKD >=USD 5,000 equivalent.
Above USD 5,000 and up to USD 10,000, obtain a bank carrying certificate before departure.
Above USD 10,000 a SAFE-issued certificate is required and is granted only in listed special cases.
Declare to CBP on arrival above USD 10,000 in aggregate.
Deposit in the US and keep the withdrawal and declaration records.
pros: $0 published counter withdrawal fee (S06 item 2.2.2.1) and no tax certificate for already-held FX cash.
Works within USD 5,000/trip without an outbound permit.
cons: USD 5,000 per trip without a certificate: 80 trips for USD 400,000 (repeat exits face stricter Huifa [2003] No. 102 limits).
Physical risk plus US forfeiture exposure for failing to file FinCEN 105 (S13).
Widest spread of any channel (notes buy/sell board rate applies for cross-currency).

name: Emigration asset transfer (移民财产转移)
who: A natural person who emigrated from mainland China (or moved to Hong Kong/Macao) and is transferring lawful pre-emigration assets (requires household-registration cancellation; most US-born individuals without former PRC hukou do not qualify).
tax_note: The transfer itself is not a tax; the tax authority's clearance on the realised assets is required and the applicable rate depends on the asset (for property, 20% of the gain under S07 Art. 3(3)).
time: 1-6 months (lump sum or batches after local SAFE approval)
docs: Written application stating the reason and a full account of source and realisation
Proof of emigration status and PRC household-registration (hukou) cancellation
Proof of ownership and realisation of the assets
PRC tax clearance certificate for the assets
steps: Apply once, to the local SAFE branch where your pre-emigration household registration was, for the whole amount you intend to move.
Settle the PRC tax position on the realised assets and obtain the tax certificate.
Obtain local SAFE branch approval: SAFE Circular Huifa [2014] No. 2 §VI cancelled the prior requirement to escalate amounts above RMB 500,000 to SAFE head office.

Remit via the designated bank directly to your own overseas account: Huifa [2014] No. 2 §VI also cancelled the 2004 multi-stage installment rule, so the bank may remit in a lump sum or in batches within the approved limit (no domestic cash payout allowed).
Keep every approval and remittance advice for the US side.
pros: The only route designed to move a whole pre-emigration balance outside the annual quota.
Lump-sum remittance permitted within the local SAFE branch's approved limit (Huifa [2014] No. 2 §VI).
cons: Requires actual emigration from Mainland China with hukou cancellation and asset realisation — generally inapplicable to US-born individuals who never held PRC hukou.
Documentary and tax-clearance burden is heavy.

name: Inheritance asset transfer (继承财产转移)
who: A foreign citizen (including a US citizen) who has inherited assets in mainland China.
tax_note: China has no inheritance tax in the instruments verified here; the estate's own tax clearance is required and is checked before conversion.
docs: Written application describing the relationship and the estate
Application form signed by you or your agent
Passport plus a certificate of overseas residence issued or authenticated by a Chinese embassy/consulate
Proof of inheritance
Proof of the deceased's title to the assets
Tax certificate or payment proof issued by the tax authority where the assets are
steps: Obtain the inheritance and title documents (Huifa [2014] No. 2 §VI(IV) simplified prior notarization rules for certain property-right/agency documents; confirm branch checklist).
Obtain the tax certificate from the tax authority where the assets are located.
File at the local SAFE branch where the decedent's household registration was (combined filing allowed for multiple decedents under Huifa [2014] No. 2 §VI(III)).
Remit in one go or in batches once approved.
Report the bequest in the US on Form 3520 if >$100,000 from a foreign estate/NRA (F07).
pros: No annual quota; lump sum permitted; combined filing available across decedents.
cons: Consular residence verification and estate tax clearance take time.
Requires local SAFE approval and source/title documentation.

name: Sale proceeds of PRC residential property
who: A US citizen selling a property they own in mainland China.
tax_note: Property transfer income is taxed at 20% of the gain (proceeds less original value and reasonable costs) under S07 Arts. 3(3) and 6(5). Whether a exemption applies to a particular flat was not verified (F06).
docs: Title certificate
Sale contract and completion documents
PRC tax payment certificate for the transfer (checked at registration under S07 Art. 15)
Proof the property was self-use where an exemption is claimed
steps: Complete the sale and settle PRC IIT: the registration authority will not transfer title without the tax clearance certificate (S07 Art. 15).
Apply to the bank/SAFE for conversion of the net proceeds under the property rules.
Convert and remit to your own US account.
Report the disposition in the US and claim the PRC tax on Form 1116.
pros: Moves a large sum in one transaction once the tax is settled.
Tax is on the gain, not the price.
cons: The 20% gain tax is the largest single number in this study.
Specific FX paperwork for a non-domestic vendor's property proceeds was not verified in this session (F06).
Months of process.

name: Dividends from a PRC company you own
who: A US citizen shareholder of a PRC company with distributable after-tax profits.
tax_note: Company-level EIT at 25% comes first (S08 Art. 4). The dividend then bears 20% domestic IIT, reduced to a 10% treaty ceiling for a US resident (S09 Arts. 9-11, S07 Art. 3(3)).
docs: Audited financial statements and profit distribution resolution
EIT payment proof
Treaty residence certification for the 10% rate
Tax withholding payment certificate
steps: Confirm distributable profits after 25% EIT and statutory reserves.
Pass the distribution resolution and withhold dividend tax at the treaty rate with the residence certificate in place.
Obtain the withholding payment certificate.
Convert and remit through the company's bank with the resolution and tax documents.
Claim the 10% withholding on Form 1116 in the US.
pros: Efficient once the company has already paid EIT.
Treaty caps the dividend tax at 10%.
cons: 25% EIT plus 10% withholding is a combined burden on the profits.
Excess withholding above the treaty rate is not creditable in the US.
Requires a company, audited accounts and a board process.

name: Overseas ATM withdrawals on a PRC bank card
who: Anyone holding a PRC-issued bank card.
tax_note: No PRC tax at withdrawal; it does not discharge unpaid tax on the underlying income.
time: about 14,000 USD per calendar year per person
docs: PRC bank card
Passport for the receiving bank's KYC
steps: Withdraw abroad within RMB 10,000 equivalent per card per day.
Stay within RMB 100,000 equivalent per person per calendar year.
Deposit the USD and keep the ATM receipts.
pros: No application and no tax certificate.
Useful for living costs, not for a balance.
cons: RMB 100,000 a year is about USD 14,000: 29 years for USD 400,000.
Exceeding the cap suspends overseas cash access for the rest of that year and the next.
ATM operator fees were not verified (F08).

name: Spend the RMB directly on overseas purchases with a PRC card
who: Anyone holding a PRC-issued card, for genuine current-account spending.
tax_note: Spending is not conversion income; it also does not settle unpaid tax on the source.
docs: PRC bank card
Merchant receipts
steps: Pay genuine overseas expenses (tuition, medical, travel, suppliers) directly with the card.
Keep invoices: the merchant is being paid, so the underlying purpose is visible.
pros: No quota and no application.
Converts at the card scheme rate as you spend.
cons: Only works if you have a matching expense stream.
Not a way to obtain USD savings.
Round-tripping purchases to extract cash can breach the cash-withdrawal rules.

name: Pay US obligations directly from the China account
who: Anyone with a genuine US invoice or obligation (tuition, hospital, tax, supplier).
tax_note: A current-account payment, not a transfer of your own savings; the tax sits with the underlying income, not with the payment.
docs: Invoice or tuition statement
Proof of the obligation
Passport
The bank's current-account payment form
steps: Obtain the genuine invoice from the US payee.
Present it at the counter with your passport; current-account payments are convertible against the underlying document (S04 Art. 12, S02 Art. 11).
Instruct the wire to the payee, not to yourself.
Keep the invoice and payment advice together.
pros: No quota and low friction when the document is genuine.
Reduces the balance you ever need to repatriate.
cons: Does not put money in your own account.
Only limited by how much genuine US spending you actually have.

name: Move RMB offshore as CNH, then convert
who: Potentially an individual eligible for cross-border RMB remittance. Eligibility for a non-resident US citizen was NOT verified in this session.
tax_note: Conversion offshore does not create PRC tax, and does not cure an untaxed onshore balance. Moving RMB out still requires a compliant onshore basis.
docs: Not established in this session - see F05
steps: Do not act on this route until the onshore basis for moving RMB to Hong Kong is confirmed in writing by the bank and, if needed, SAFE.
If a basis exists, convert in the offshore market and remit USD to the US.
pros: Offshore spreads are typically narrower.
HSBC group transfers can be free for Premier.
cons: Eligibility for a non-resident individual was not verified.
Guessing the basis is exactly how people end up in an Art. 39 or Art. 45 case.
Separate offshore account opening and KYC.

name: Sell RMB privately to someone who wants USD (private FX swap)
who: Not lawful for anyone.
tax_note: Not a tax question.
steps: Do not do this. S04 Art. 45 covers private, disguised and brokered FX trading: confiscation of the proceeds plus a fine of up to 30% of the amount, or 30%-100% if serious, with criminal liability for larger cases.
pros: None that survives contact with Art. 45.
cons: Confiscation plus a fine up to the value of the amount.
Criminal exposure.
Counterparty risk with no recourse.

name: Underground bank / 'huipiao' (offshore RMB, onshore settlement)
who: Not lawful for anyone.
tax_note: Not a tax question.
steps: Do not do this. It is the paradigm case of Art. 39 evasion and Art. 45 illegal FX trading, and is prosecuted as illegal business operation at scale.
pros: None.
cons: Funds are typically seized.
Fines of 30%-100% and criminal liability.
No legal recourse if the operator disappears.

name: Buy crypto or USDT in China and sell abroad
who: Not lawful for anyone in China.
tax_note: Not a tax question.
steps: Do not do this. Yin Fa [2026] No. 42 (which replaced Yin Fa [2021] No. 237) states that exchanging legal tender for virtual currency is an illegal financial activity, that institutions may not provide settlement services for it, and that losses are borne by the participant.
pros: None that is lawful.
cons: Illegal financial activity
No recourse, and exchanges are blocked from RMB rails.
Creates a US tax and reporting mess on top.

name: Borrow a relative's or friend's USD 50,000 quota
who: Not lawful for anyone.
tax_note: Not a tax question.
steps: Do not do this. S01 Art. 7 prohibits splitting to evade limits and S04 Arts. 39–40 supply statutory fines up to 30% (30%–100% if serious) plus criminal liability. Note: the older 'watch list' notice S18 has conflicting active/repealed mirror labels (F03), so S01 Art. 7 and S04 are the operative authorities.
pros: None.
cons: Statutory fines up to the amount involved and refusal of bank counter service.
Both sides exposed, including your relative.
The annual purchase quota may not even apply to you (see F02).

name: Present fabricated contracts or invoices to the bank
who: Not lawful for anyone.
tax_note: Not a tax question.
steps: Do not do this. S01 Art. 7 prohibits tampering with authenticity administration using fabricated vouchers; S04 Arts. 39-40 provide fines of up to 30% (or 30%-100% if serious) plus criminal liability.
pros: None.
cons: Fines up to the value of the amount moved.
Criminal record.
The bank keeps the documents for at least five years.

name: Keep the money in China and use it as a spending account
who: Anyone — this is the baseline every other route must beat.
tax_note: No conversion, no PRC conversion cost. US reporting duties (FBAR/8938) still apply.
docs: Passport for account maintenance
FBAR / Form 8938 filings
steps: Keep the balance and spend it on trips, cards and obligations paid from China.
File FBAR and Form 8938 every year the thresholds are met.
Revisit only if you need the capital in USD.
pros: Zero conversion cost and zero spread.
Reversible at any time.
cons: Currency and country risk stay with you.
US reporting continues regardless.
The problem is deferred, not solved.
